newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan protests Russian Cossack border units.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan protests Russian Cossack border units.

text.p: Kazakhstan issued an official protest on Wednesday over what it called a decision by Russia to deploy armed Cossack units along their common frontier.

"Serious concern has been provoked by an experiment by Russia's federal border service which will place paramilitary units made up from Cossack formations along the border," a foreign ministry statement said.
It said Russia's federal border service had established a new "border watch directorate" to oversee the deployment of Cossack units along the Russian-Kazakh frontier.
The two ex-Soviet states share a border of about 5,000 km (3,100 miles) which has not been clearly defined, like many of the frontiers between the members of the Commonwealth of Independent States.
The Cossacks are a warrior class of ethnic Slavs which spearheaded Russian expansion in Tsarist times and have enjoyed a revival since the collapse of the Soviet Union.

A spokesman for Russia's border guards service told Reuters in Moscow that the experiment, which started about four months ago, involved volunteers and they were not only Cossacks. There were no regular border guard units on the frontier.
Spokesman Alexander Suvorov added that the patrols were not armed but in future they might be because "there are so many irregularities, mostly in drugs and smuggling".
He said his service had been inviting the Kazakh side to work together over the frontier to prevent spreading crime.
The Kazakh statement said Russia's plans were a "serious breach" of existing accords between the two states, both of which are members of a fast-crumbling customs union with Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.
The Kazakh-Russian frontier, populated mainly by Russians and Ukrainians, is ethnically charged.
Many Russians believe northern Kazakhstan, rich in metals, oil and the Central Asian state's grain belt, is really Russian territory.

Keen to anchor its rich but desolate northern steppe land politically, Kazakhstan -- itself the size of western Europe -- is moving its capital this year from Almaty in the southeast to Akmola in the north.
President Nursultan Nazarbayev has brushed aside diplomats' doubts over the move, saying he will toast the New Year there at the end of 1997.
Because of its large Russian population and almost total reliance on Russian pipelines for the export of its oil wealth, Kazakhstan is normally very cautious in its relations with the Kremlin.

But digging in its heels over the Cossack issue, and a quiet but determined fight with Russia for title to vast oil reserves along its Caspian Sea coastline in the west, has seen Almaty take an increasingly assertive line.
